dek.text: The state built a network of Flock plate reader cameras with a fee on auto insurance, then paused the money. Texas towns are now deciding whether to pay for the cameras themselves.

introduction.text: [In {{number:c15}} the Legislature unanimously added ${{number:c15:1}} to Texans' auto insurance to fight catalytic converter theft](c15). [The Motor Vehicle Crime Prevention Authority turned that fee into at least {{number:c17:1}} Flock cameras](c17), [and a Tribune analysis found it put at least ${{number:c16}} million of the fee toward the network](c16).

[Then the Governor ordered every state agency to pause funding for Flock cameras, which the Tribune called AI-powered surveillance devices](c12). [His spokesman confirmed the order in an article dated {{date:c13}}](c13). [Any state agency providing money is making clear its funds can't be used for the cameras](c14). The camera on the pole is now a line in each town's own budget, and the towns are not answering alike.

paragraphs.text: [At least {{number:c1}} cities and counties have shut off more than {{number:c1:1}} Flock cameras since the state money was rescinded in late August, the Tribune reported](c1). [Plano, Robinson and Kendall County ended their contracts entirely](c5). [Houston and Dallas shut their grant funded cameras and kept much of their networks running](c6). The two counts come from different articles and different populations, so neither is a share of the other.

[On {{date:c32}} the El Paso City Council directed the removal within {{number:c32}} days of every Flock fixed camera on city property and right of way](c32). [It also directed the city manager not to enter or renew any contract with Flock or any other provider of fixed plate reader cameras](c33). [Leander's council directed the city to stop funding its Flock contract](c20), [and its police stopped using Flock cameras and Flock data as of {{date:c21}}](c21), [in the city's words "in response to community concerns"](c22).

[Kyle's {{number:c8}} grant has not arrived, and part of it would help pay for {{number:c8:3}} Flock cameras](c8). [Its council voted {{number:c9}} to {{number:c9:1}} to keep the contract anyway](c9).

[The College Station City Council voted {{number:c23}} to {{number:c23:1}} on {{date:c23}} to keep two Flock agreements, one for cameras on state highway roads and one for cameras on other roads](c23). [Its police chief put the case plainly. "You can't afford the number of cops it would take to do what this system is doing"](c7). [The city says no search of the system can be made without reasonable suspicion](c27), [and that it keeps every search with no end date](c28). [It reports property crime fell over the same months and says the drop correlates with the cameras](c31). Correlation is the city's word, and it is not a finding that the cameras caused the drop.

[Laredo's council voted {{number:c2}} to {{number:c2:1}} to put the question to a nonbinding referendum in May](c2). [Voters will be asked whether to spend ${{number:c3}} million a year to keep {{number:c3:1}} cameras running in city limits](c3). [The mayor said the city's residents should have a chance to say whether local taxpayers fund the whole system](c4).

[League City's council called its own vote before the pause, on {{date:c34}}](c34). [Its ballot asks, as a nonbinding statement of voter preference, whether police should keep using fixed plate reader cameras on public roadways](c35). [That election is on {{date:c36}}](c36).

sections.heading: What the record can't yet say

paragraphs.text: [The articles print no calendar date for the Governor's order, only that it came on a Thursday night](c13), [and none for Laredo's vote, only a Monday night](c2). [College Station describes the cameras as solar powered and LTE connected, photographing the rear of passing vehicles by day and by night](c25), [and sorting each vehicle's make, model and color from the image](c26). This record carries no retention period for the camera images and no list of the cities and counties in the Tribune's count.
